Session-end condensation could make a checkpoint durable before its updated session state was saved. If the hook was killed in that window, recovery still considered the transcript unfinished and could write it again under a different checkpoint ID. On current `main`, the immediate `PostCommit` path described in the issue no longer reproduces this for a no-files session because that path discards it. The durable failure still reproduces through `entire doctor`, which sees the ended session as unfinished and previously generated a new checkpoint ID for the same transcript range. ### Approach This PR uses a write-ahead checkpoint ID. It saves the intended ID as `CondensationAttemptID`, writes the checkpoint with that ID, advances the session bookkeeping, and then clears the pending attempt. If the process dies after the write, the next attempt reuses the same ID instead of creating a duplicate. The reservation is also honored during commit preparation and `PostCommit`. If `PostCommit` receives a different checkpoint ID, it preserves the interrupted session and shadow branch rather than overwriting its recovery state. Advancing `LastCheckpointID` or `CheckpointTranscriptStart` before writing would prevent duplication but introduce a data-loss window: state could claim that a transcript was saved when the checkpoint write had failed. The pending ID records durable intent without claiming that the write succeeded. `CondensationRecoveryPending` separately records when recovery may need to reconcile an interrupted write created by an older CLI version. This keeps the more expensive storage lookup out of normal condensation paths. Reserved writes are routed using their checkpoint ID format. If checkpoint configuration changes between reservation and retry, the checkpoint is still written to the backend that originally generated its ID. ### Recovering state from older CLI versions Older interrupted sessions have no pending checkpoint ID. Doctor reconciles them using the session identity, transcript bounds and content, checkpoint counts, agent and turn metadata, touched files, and session kind. Externalized images are reinserted before comparing transcripts. Storage listing or reading failures stop recovery and preserve its state for another retry rather than being treated as “checkpoint not found.” If the session has genuinely advanced, recovery creates a new checkpoint instead of reusing the older one. ### Related findings `checkpoint list` exposes both duplicates because they have different checkpoint IDs, while `tokens profile` can count both and inflate checkpoint-observed token totals. The latter already warns about overlapping checkpoint history. Codex kills timed-out hook process groups with `SIGKILL`, not `SIGTERM`, so Entire cannot print its normal termination message during a Codex timeout. See Codex’s [hook runner](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/bb701f1e8c8db884fa0cdafff4b8dcb1604f2fdd/codex-rs/hooks/src/engine/command_runner.rs) and [process-group cleanup](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/bb701f1e8c8db884fa0cdafff4b8dcb1604f2fdd/codex-rs/utils/pty/src/process_group.rs). ### Follow-up plan This PR lands the non-destructive part first: it prevents new duplicate checkpoints, makes retries deterministic, and reconciles interrupted writes from older CLI versions. It deliberately does not remove or hide duplicate pairs that already exist. Questions for a follow-up: 1. Should existing duplicate pairs remain as physical history and be collapsed only in `checkpoint list` and `tokens profile`, or should `doctor` repair the stored history? 2. If one checkpoint becomes canonical, which should win: the original session-end write or the later recovery write? What should happen when their metadata differs? 3. Should repair be automatic, an explicit doctor action, or reporting-only until the user chooses? 4. Should transcript-range idempotency become a shared rule for every condensation entry point, or remain limited to session-end and doctor recovery? Once those product choices are clear, existing duplicates can be handled separately without coupling destructive cleanup or changed read semantics to this durability fix. ### Verification Regression coverage includes pending ID reuse, legacy orphan reconciliation, repeated storage read failures, recovery-marker persistence, mismatched commit IDs, backend changes between reservation and retry, and advanced sessions receiving a genuinely new checkpoint. - [x] `mise run check` - [x] Lint completed with 0 issues - [x] Race-enabled unit and integration tests passed - [x] Vogon canary passed — 56/56 - [x] Roger-Roger canary passed — 4/4 ### API Notes `api/checkpoint.WriteRequest` adds `ReservedSession` for writes whose checkpoint ID was previously persisted. Session state adds the optional `CondensationAttemptID` and `CondensationRecoveryPending` fields. ### Compatibility / Release Notes Existing session-state files remain compatible because the new fields are optional. Existing duplicate checkpoints are not removed, hidden, or rewritten, and `checkpoint list` and `tokens profile` behavior is unchanged. Session-end condensation could make a checkpoint durable before its updated session state was saved. If the hook was killed in that window, recovery still considered the transcript unfinished and could write it again under a different checkpoint ID. On current `main`, the immediate `PostCommit` path described in the issue no longer reproduces this for a no-files session because that path discards it. The durable failure still reproduces through `entire doctor`, which sees the ended session as unfinished and previously generated a new checkpoint ID for the same transcript range. ### Approach This PR uses a write-ahead checkpoint ID. It saves the intended ID as `CondensationAttemptID`, writes the checkpoint with that ID, advances the session bookkeeping, and then clears the pending attempt. If the process dies after the write, the next attempt reuses the same ID instead of creating a duplicate. The reservation is also honored during commit preparation and `PostCommit`. If `PostCommit` receives a different checkpoint ID, it preserves the interrupted session and shadow branch rather than overwriting its recovery state. Advancing `LastCheckpointID` or `CheckpointTranscriptStart` before writing would prevent duplication but introduce a data-loss window: state could claim that a transcript was saved when the checkpoint write had failed. The pending ID records durable intent without claiming that the write succeeded. `CondensationRecoveryPending` separately records when recovery may need to reconcile an interrupted write created by an older CLI version. This keeps the more expensive storage lookup out of normal condensation paths. Reserved writes are routed using their checkpoint ID format. If checkpoint configuration changes between reservation and retry, the checkpoint is still written to the backend that originally generated its ID. ### Recovering state from older CLI versions Older interrupted sessions have no pending checkpoint ID. Doctor reconciles them using the session identity, transcript bounds and content, checkpoint counts, agent and turn metadata, touched files, and session kind. Externalized images are reinserted before comparing transcripts. Storage listing or reading failures stop recovery and preserve its state for another retry rather than being treated as “checkpoint not found.” If the session has genuinely advanced, recovery creates a new checkpoint instead of reusing the older one. ### Related findings `checkpoint list` exposes both duplicates because they have different checkpoint IDs, while `tokens profile` can count both and inflate checkpoint-observed token totals. The latter already warns about overlapping checkpoint history. Codex kills timed-out hook process groups with `SIGKILL`, not `SIGTERM`, so Entire cannot print its normal termination message during a Codex timeout. See Codex’s [hook runner](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/bb701f1e8c8db884fa0cdafff4b8dcb1604f2fdd/codex-rs/hooks/src/engine/command_runner.rs) and [process-group cleanup](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/bb701f1e8c8db884fa0cdafff4b8dcb1604f2fdd/codex-rs/utils/pty/src/process_group.rs). ### Follow-up plan This PR lands the non-destructive part first: it prevents new duplicate checkpoints, makes retries deterministic, and reconciles interrupted writes from older CLI versions. Thanks! # PR #2052 fix(codex): use repository hook root in linked worktrees ## Description Fixes #2020. Codex 0.149.0 can load project hooks from a different checkout than the one in which it is running. In a conventional linked worktree, its app-server `hooks/list` response reports the primary checkout's `.codex/hooks.json`; a divergent file present only in the linked worktree is not loaded. This PR makes that effective location visible without giving Entire ownership of another checkout. Discovery and mutation are deliberately separate: Entire may inspect the file Codex actually loads, but installs, removes, and cleans hooks only in the exact checkout where the command was invoked. ## Discovery and ownership - `WorktreeHooksPath` identifies `/.codex/hooks.json`. It is the only mutation target used by install, uninstall, presence, freshness, deselection, and clean flows. - `DiscoveredHooksPath` identifies the project hooks file Codex is expected to load. It is used only for read-only configuration and trust diagnostics. - `ResolveHookDiscovery` consumes the shared `gitrepo.ResolveGitLayout` classification rather than maintaining a Codex-specific `.git`, `commondir`, or worktree-marker parser. - Conventional linked worktrees discover the primary checkout's hook file. Normal checkouts, ordinary submodules, and separate-Git-directory checkouts discover their own hook file. - `.bare/worktrees`, linked submodules, contradictory metadata, and other behavior not pinned against Codex are reported as unresolved. Entire does not claim an unsupported layout or guess a writable fallback. `HookDiscovery` carries no write target, migration path, cleanup path, or lock path. Its `RepositoryWide` bit describes the reach of the configuration Codex discovers; it does not authorize repository-wide mutation. ## Checkout-local mutation `entire enable`, `entire agent remove codex`, agent deselection, and `entire clean` mutate only the current checkout's `.codex/hooks.json`. They do not create another checkout's `.codex` directory, migrate a worktree-local file into the primary checkout, remove a discovered file owned elsewhere, or perform repository-wide cleanup. Concurrent updates are serialized only with `/.codex/hooks.json.lock`. There is no `entire-codex-hooks.lock` in the Git common directory and no synchronization across worktrees. An old common-directory lock, if present from a previous build, is neither used nor cleaned from another checkout. Current-checkout writes are hardened before the final atomic replacement: - the logical target must be exactly `/.codex/hooks.json`; - redirected `.codex` directories, final-file symlinks, non-regular files, unrelated destinations, and Git-metadata redirection are rejected; - existing user hooks, unknown hook events, and unrelated top-level fields are preserved; - uninstall removes only Entire-managed entries; - an existing file keeps its permission bits, while a new file uses `0600`. ## Bounded read-only inspection The local and discovered files are inspected independently as absent, user-only, Entire-managed, invalid, or unresolved. Inspection is contained to the exact canonical `.codex` directory, requires a stable regular file, caps `hooks.json` at 1 MiB, reads through a limit with one overflow byte, and checks file identity before and after the read. It never creates a directory, rewrites configuration, removes entries, or acquires a mutation lock. The structured inspection also reports whether the core Entire events are present, which current events are missing, whether managed commands and timeouts match this CLI, whether the current checkout has the project layer Codex requires, whether local trust records were readable, and which declared hooks lack an approval record. Entire does not compute, copy, or synthesize Codex trust hashes. ## Diagnostics and remedy - `entire doctor` reports the current-worktree path and Codex-discovered path, invalid or unresolved discovery, a missing project layer, managed hook drift, and trust gaps. - `entire status` keeps current-checkout installation/freshness semantics separate from effective Codex discovery and exposes the mismatch under the existing `codex_hooks` JSON object without changing the warning wording established in this PR. - SessionStart appends a short, bounded, read-only discovery or trust warning when applicable. When hooks exist only in a linked worktree, Entire does not repair the primary checkout automatically. The user-owned remedy is to commit `.codex/hooks.json` and apply that commit to the primary checkout (typically by cherry-pick), or run `entire enable` from the primary checkout. Because linked worktrees share Git objects, the commit is immediately available to cherry-pick; no push or fetch is required. ## Pinned Codex integration contract `TestCodexAppServerHooksList_LinkedWorktreeUsesPrimaryCheckout` is a no-model integration test pinned to `@openai/codex@0.149.0`. It: 1. creates a normal repository and conventional linked worktree with distinct hook markers; 2. starts `codex app-server` in the linked worktree with an isolated `CODEX_HOME`; 3. sends `initialize`, `initialized`, and `hooks/list` JSONL messages over stdio; 4. requires the primary marker and primary `sourcePath`; 5. rejects the linked-only marker; and 6. requires empty `warnings` and `errors`. The test makes no model request and needs no OpenAI credentials. Local integration runs skip when the exact Codex binary is unavailable. CI installs version 0.149.0 and sets `ENTIRE_TEST_REQUIRE_CODEX_APP_SERVER=1`, so a missing binary or version drift fails rather than silently skipping. ## Verification status The implementation includes focused unit coverage for Git-layout classification, path-role separation, current-checkout-only install/remove/clean behavior, exact-worktree locking, destination containment, symlink refusal, bounded reads, mode preservation, doctor/status/SessionStart diagnostics, trust inspection, and JSON output, plus the pinned app-server integration contract above. I corrected two merged comments that still described `PostCommit` as the general retry path. ### My current understanding A session is the lifecycle record for an agent interaction. It is separate from the transcript. Entire creates session state at turn start with its identity, phase, base commit, timestamps, and agent metadata. At that point, `StepCount` is zero and the transcript may not exist yet. `StepCount` tracks temporary checkpoint steps. It increments only after Entire successfully writes a temporary step, and it resets to zero after successful condensation. It does not measure transcript length or tell us whether the session contains useful work. Checkpoint content can come from the parent transcript, touched files, or subagent task records. A task-only session can have no parent transcript, no shadow branch, and `StepCount == 0`, but still contain a task record pointing to a subagent transcript, files, labels, and token data. That session must still be condensed. Only a session with no transcript, no touched files, and no task records is empty. The ownership split is: - If an ended session has files waiting for a user commit, session-end condensation leaves it alone. Once Git creates the commit, `PostCommit` reads the `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer and condenses the session against that commit. - If an ended session has no pending files but has transcript or task content, the session-end path eagerly condenses it. - If eager condensation is interrupted, `entire doctor` recovers it. `PostCommit` must not attach the interrupted session to the next unrelated commit. Doctor remains human-triggered unless it runs with `--force`. - If the session has no meaningful content, condensation skips it instead of writing a metadata-only checkpoint. I understand `CondensationAttemptID` as write-ahead identity. Entire reserves the checkpoint ID before the potentially interruptible write. If the process dies after writing the checkpoint but before saving the completed state, recovery reuses the same ID instead of creating another checkpoint over the same transcript range. There are two synchronization concerns. The state lock prevents two processes from modifying the same session file concurrently. Separately, the reservation and condensation paths must make the same eligibility decision. Sharing `prepareEagerCondensation` prevents one path from reserving an ID while the other skips the session and leaves a stale reservation behind. Condensation and `PostCommit` write the fast regex-redacted blobs. OPF is the network-backed privacy pass and stays in the pre-push rewrite, where Entire processes the pending checkpoint blobs in one batch. If an OPF run is selected and fails, the push path withholds those checkpoint refs rather than marking them as OPF-processed. Please correct me if any of these lifecycle, ownership, or recovery boundaries are off. --- PR #2038 COMMENT MuskanPaliwal 2026-08-21T08:10:23Z The PR is now ready for a review @Soph. Task-only sessions remain condensable with `StepCount == 0` and no shadow branch. I corrected two merged comments that still described `PostCommit` as the general retry path. ### My current understanding A session is the lifecycle record for an agent interaction. It is separate from the transcript. Entire creates session state at turn start with its identity, phase, base commit, timestamps, and agent metadata. At that point, `StepCount` is zero and the transcript may not exist yet. `StepCount` tracks temporary checkpoint steps. It increments only after Entire successfully writes a temporary step, and it resets to zero after successful condensation. It does not measure transcript length or tell us whether the session contains useful work. Checkpoint content can come from the parent transcript, touched files, or subagent task records. A task-only session can have no parent transcript, no shadow branch, and `StepCount == 0`, but still contain a task record pointing to a subagent transcript, files, labels, and token data. That session must still be condensed. Only a session with no transcript, no touched files, and no task records is empty. The ownership split is: - If an ended session has files waiting for a user commit, session-end condensation leaves it alone. Once Git creates the commit, `PostCommit` reads the `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer and condenses the session against that commit. - If an ended session has no pending files but has transcript or task content, the session-end path eagerly condenses it. - If eager condensation is interrupted, `entire doctor` recovers it. `PostCommit` must not attach the interrupted session to the next unrelated commit. Doctor remains human-triggered unless it runs with `--force`. - If the session has no meaningful content, condensation skips it instead of writing a metadata-only checkpoint. I understand `CondensationAttemptID` as write-ahead identity. Entire reserves the checkpoint ID before the potentially interruptible write. If the process dies after writing the checkpoint but before saving the completed state, recovery reuses the same ID instead of creating another checkpoint over the same transcript range. There are two synchronization concerns. The state lock prevents two processes from modifying the same session file concurrently. Separately, the reservation and condensation paths must make the same eligibility decision. Sharing `prepareEagerCondensation` prevents one path from reserving an ID while the other skips the session and leaves a stale reservation behind. Condensation and `PostCommit` write the fast regex-redacted blobs. OPF is the network-backed privacy pass and stays in the pre-push rewrite, where Entire processes the pending checkpoint blobs in one batch. If an OPF run is selected and fails, the push path withholds those checkpoint refs rather than marking them as OPF-processed. Task-only sessions remain condensable with `StepCount == 0` and no shadow branch. I corrected two merged comments that still described `PostCommit` as the general retry path. ### My current understanding A session is the lifecycle record for an agent interaction. It is separate from the transcript. Entire creates session state at turn start with its identity, phase, base commit, timestamps, and agent metadata. At that point, `StepCount` is zero and the transcript may not exist yet. `StepCount` tracks temporary checkpoint steps. It increments only after Entire successfully writes a temporary step, and it resets to zero after successful condensation. It does not measure transcript length or tell us whether the session contains useful work. Checkpoint content can come from the parent transcript, touched files, or subagent task records. A task-only session can have no parent transcript, no shadow branch, and `StepCount == 0`, but still contain a task record pointing to a subagent transcript, files, labels, and token data. That session must still be condensed. Only a session with no transcript, no touched files, and no task records is empty. The ownership split is: - If an ended session has files waiting for a user commit, session-end condensation leaves it alone. Once Git creates the commit, `PostCommit` reads the `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer and condenses the session against that commit. - If an ended session has no pending files but has transcript or task content, the session-end path eagerly condenses it. - If eager condensation is interrupted, `entire doctor` recovers it. `PostCommit` must not attach the interrupted session to the next unrelated commit. Doctor remains human-triggered unless it runs with `--force`. - If the session has no meaningful content, condensation skips it instead of writing a metadata-only checkpoint. I understand `CondensationAttemptID` as write-ahead identity. Entire reserves the checkpoint ID before the potentially interruptible write. If the process dies after writing the checkpoint but before saving the completed state, recovery reuses the same ID instead of creating another checkpoint over the same transcript range. There are two synchronization concerns. The state lock prevents two processes from modifying the same session file concurrently. Separately, the reservation and condensation paths must make the same eligibility decision. Sharing `prepareEagerCondensation` prevents one path from reserving an ID while the other skips the session and leaves a stale reservation behind. Condensation and `PostCommit` write the fast regex-redacted blobs. OPF is the network-backed privacy pass and stays in the pre-push rewrite, where Entire processes the pending checkpoint blobs in one batch. If an OPF run is selected and fails, the push path withholds those checkpoint refs rather than marking them as OPF-processed. It is separate from the transcript. Entire creates session state at turn start with its identity, phase, base commit, timestamps, and agent metadata. At that point, `StepCount` is zero and the transcript may not exist yet. `StepCount` tracks temporary checkpoint steps. It increments only after Entire successfully writes a temporary step, and it resets to zero after successful condensation. It does not measure transcript length or tell us whether the session contains useful work. Checkpoint content can come from the parent transcript, touched files, or subagent task records. A task-only session can have no parent transcript, no shadow branch, and `StepCount == 0`, but still contain a task record pointing to a subagent transcript, files, labels, and token data. That session must still be condensed. Only a session with no transcript, no touched files, and no task records is empty. The ownership split is: - If an ended session has files waiting for a user commit, session-end condensation leaves it alone. Once Git creates the commit, `PostCommit` reads the `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer and condenses the session against that commit. - If an ended session has no pending files but has transcript or task content, the session-end path eagerly condenses it. - If eager condensation is interrupted, `entire doctor` recovers it. `PostCommit` must not attach the interrupted session to the next unrelated commit. Doctor remains human-triggered unless it runs with `--force`. - If the session has no meaningful content, condensation skips it instead of writing a metadata-only checkpoint. I understand `CondensationAttemptID` as write-ahead identity. Entire reserves the checkpoint ID before the potentially interruptible write. If the process dies after writing the checkpoint but before saving the completed state, recovery reuses the same ID instead of creating another checkpoint over the same transcript range. There are two synchronization concerns. The state lock prevents two processes from modifying the same session file concurrently. Separately, the reservation and condensation paths must make the same eligibility decision. Sharing `prepareEagerCondensation` prevents one path from reserving an ID while the other skips the session and leaves a stale reservation behind. Condensation and `PostCommit` write the fast regex-redacted blobs. OPF is the network-backed privacy pass and stays in the pre-push rewrite, where Entire processes the pending checkpoint blobs in one batch. If an OPF run is selected and fails, the push path withholds those checkpoint refs rather than marking them as OPF-processed. PR #1901 Copilot cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent.go
FINDING: In writeTranscript's TranscriptPath fallback, the transcript is redacted before being sanitized. That reintroduces the original performance/correctness problem for callers that reach the store via TranscriptPath (e.g. import): the redaction scan still processes ciphertext that sanitization would later discard, and the stored-copy pipeline order no longer matches sanitize → … → redact. Sanitizing the raw bytes before calling redact.JSONLBytes keeps the intended ordering while still ensuring untrusted disk content is redacted before storage.
REPLY: Fixed in bd574bfbd — that block now sanitizes before `redact.JSONLBytes`.

PR #1901 Copilot docs/architecture/sessions-and-checkpoints.md
FINDING: This section states that the Stop (shadow branch) path follows the full sanitize → externalize images → redact pipeline, but the Stop path in lifecycle.go only sanitizes before writing full.jsonl; the shadow-branch capture/redaction path (metadata directory walker) does not externalize images. As written, this can mislead future changes (e.g. assuming images are preserved in shadow transcripts). Consider documenting the shadow-branch behavior separately and limiting the 3-step pipeline claim to the committed-checkpoint/finalize paths where image externalization actually runs.
REPLY: Good catch — this was my error, fixed in bd574bfbd.

PR #1906 Copilot cmd/entire/cli/agent/external/discovery.go
FINDING: `discoverAndRegisterNamed` still reassigns `ctx` to the derived timeout context. Even though you keep `callerCtx`, reusing the `ctx` identifier makes it easy to accidentally consult the wrong context again later (this bug was caused by `ctx` shadowing). Consider keeping `ctx` as the caller context and using a separate name (e.g. `discoveryCtx`) for the derived timeout context.
REPLY: Good call — done in c5d953caa. `ctx` now stays the caller's throughout and the derived context is `discoveryCtx`.

PR #1908 Copilot cmd/entire/cli/search_cmd_test.go
FINDING: This test sets ENTIRE_CODE_SEARCH via t.Setenv, but the --compact/--code incompatibility is checked before code-search gating is evaluated, so the env tweak is unnecessary. Dropping it allows the test to use t.Parallel() and avoid serializing the whole file’s test execution.
REPLY: Fixed in 1973acce2 — dropped the env tweak and the test now runs with t.Parallel().

PR #1919 cursor[bot] e2e/tests/codex_resume_test.go
FINDING: ### Closing session deletes its Codex home
REPLY: Good catch — confirmed and fixed in 73b9c76a4. `Close()` runs the OnClose cleanup that `RemoveAll`s the isolated CODEX_HOME, which the resume flow still needs. Added `TmuxSession.Terminate()` (kills the process to release the writer lock, but skips cleanups) and the test now uses it and removes the home itself via `t.Cleanup` at test end.

PR #1919 Copilot e2e/tests/codex_resume_test.go
FINDING: codexSession.Close() will also delete the isolated CODEX_HOME directory because Codex.StartSession registers a RemoveAll cleanup via TmuxSession.OnClose (see e2e/agents/codex.go:146-166 and e2e/agents/tmux.go:239-242). This test continues to reuse codexSession.Home() for `entire resume`, for locating the restored rollout, and for `codexAgent.ResumeSession`, which assumes CODEX_HOME is still seeded (config.toml/auth.json/trust state). Closing here therefore wipes the Codex home and can break the remainder of the test or make it behave differently than intended.
REPLY: Good catch — confirmed and fixed in 73b9c76a4. `Close()` runs the OnClose cleanup that `RemoveAll`s the isolated CODEX_HOME, which the resume flow still needs. Added `TmuxSession.Terminate()` (kills the process to release the writer lock, but skips cleanups) and the test now uses it and removes the home itself via `t.Cleanup` at test end.

FINDING: ### Worktree re-exec masks child exits
REPLY: Fixed in b989d612c. Child failures are now returned as a SilentError because the child already rendered its own error, and parent-context cancellation is propagated as a wrapped context error so signal handling remains quiet.

PR #1921 cursor[bot] cmd/entire/cli/review/target.go

PR #1921 cursor[bot] cmd/entire/cli/review_target.go
FINDING: ### Branch targets require trail remote

PR #1921 Copilot cmd/entire/cli/trail_checkout_worktree.go
FINDING: When reusing an existing worktree, validation is only performed for managed worktrees. PR #1930 Copilot cmd/entire/cli/agent_group.go
FINDING: `external.DiscoverAndRegisterAlways` scans every `entire-agent-*` on $PATH and executes each binary’s `info` subcommand (via `external.New`). For `entire agent add <name>`, this is broader than necessary and can unexpectedly execute unrelated external-agent binaries. Prefer discovering only the requested agent via `external.DiscoverAndRegisterNamedAlways` and returning its error so failures aren’t masked as “Unknown agent”.

PR #1932 Copilot cmd/entire/cli/telemetry/detached.go

PR #2068 Copilot cmd/entire/cli/state.go
FINDING: RememberAgentTaskLink() treats taskToolUseID as required, but ValidateToolUseID allows an empty string. That means this function can write an agent-task link file with an empty tool_use_id, which LookupAgentTaskLink will never return (it rejects empty ToolUseID), so the link is silently unusable.
REPLY: Fixed in 8015d6574 — RememberAgentTaskLink now rejects an empty taskToolUseID explicitly before validation.

Grok stores part of a reasoning record like this:

```json
{
  "type": "reasoning",
  "summary": [{"text": "Inspect the repository"}],

}
```

`encrypted_content` is an opaque, replay-critical payload. Entire does not need to understand it, but Grok expects the restored value to be exactly the same bytes.

Think of it like a wax seal on an envelope:

- Entire cannot read or recreate the seal.
- Grok validates the seal when resuming.
- Changing even one character invalidates it.

### Why Entire corrupted it

The redaction path looked roughly like this:

```text
JSONLContent
    ↓
parse each JSON record
    ↓
walk each string field
    ↓
shouldSkipJSONLField("encrypted_content")
    ↓ false
scan value for secrets
    ↓
entropy detector sees random-looking base64
    ↓
replace suspicious segments with REDACTED
```

Encrypted and cryptographically signed values deliberately look random. Unfortunately, API keys and tokens also look random.

So the entropy scanner cannot distinguish these two values by their bytes alone:

```text

Opaque attestation: REDACTED...
```

Before our fix, the result became:

```json

  "encrypted_content": "REDACTED/I5E9cLXoEZ7MtARRP9vN"
}

Entire then stored that corrupted transcript. On restoration, Grok tried to validate the payload, found that it no longer matched, and rejected the entire conversation as incompatible.

Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using hybrid search (semantic + keyword),
powered by the Entire search service.

Requires authentication via 'entire login' (GitHub device flow).

By default, results are scoped to the current repository. Use --all-repos to
search across all accessible repos.

Run without arguments to open an interactive search. Results are
displayed in an interactive table. Use --json for machine-readable output,
and add --compact for a trimmed per-result shape suited to agents (implies
--json): id, type, repo, branch, author, date, files touched, score, match
snippet, and a truncated title instead of the full prompt (repo hits add
description and checkpoint count). Fetch full detail
for a single result with 'entire checkpoint explain <id>', or add --full to
that command to pull the checkpoint's entire session transcript. For a
checkpoint hit from another GitHub repo, add --repo <owner/name> to
'entire checkpoint explain' (requires the full checkpoint ID; unrelated to
this command's --repo filter below).

CLI queries also support inline filters like author:<name>, date:<week|month>,
branch:<name>, repo:<owner/name>, and repo:* to search all accessible repos.

Usage:
  entire search [query] [flags]

Examples:
  entire search "retry backoff" --json
  entire search "retry backoff" --json --compact
  entire search "auth timeout author:alice date:week"
  entire search --code "parseToken"

Flags:
      --all-repos        Search all accessible repos instead of just the current one
      --author string    Filter by author name
      --branch string    Filter by branch name
      --case-sensitive   Case-sensitive code search (only with --code)
      --code             Search code content across repositories
      --compact          Trimmed JSON output for agents: id, repo, files touched, score, match snippet, and a truncated title instead of the full prompt (implies --json)
      --date string      Filter by time period (week or month)
  -h, --help             help for search
      --json             Output as JSON
      --limit int        Maximum number of results (per page for checkpoint search, total for --code) (default 10)
      --page int         Page number (1-based) (default 1)
      --repo strings     Filter by repository (gh/owner/repo, et/proj/repo, owner/repo, ULID, or *); repeatable and comma-separated for multiple repos

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only, instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

const patch = "*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: PR-REVIEW-RETROSPECTIVE.md
+# Entire CLI PR review retrospective
+
+## The central finding
+
+Your main risk is not Go syntax. It is changing one part of a system before you have mapped the ownership, state transitions, failure modes, and recovery path around it.
+
+The strongest review comments repeatedly found one of these problems:
+
+- two code paths made the same decision with slightly different predicates;
+- a local fix changed behavior at a wider persistence or mutation boundary;
+- an error such as unreadable, invalid, or canceled was collapsed into absent or successful;
+- a test exercised a nearby abstraction but not the production failure;
+- a comment, status message, or PR description claimed more than the code guaranteed;
+- a new path resolver, state classifier, or helper duplicated an existing one;
+- a large PR combined discovery, mutation, migration, diagnostics, and integration work before the contract was settled.
+
+This is good news. The reviews do not show a recurring inability to write Go. They show that your next level is systems reasoning: seeing the whole state machine before editing one transition.
+
+## Research scope
+
+This report uses GitHub data collected on 2026-08-31. August figures are month-to-date at the collection time.
+
+- I inspected all nine closed PRs authored by `MuskanPaliwal` in `entireio/cli`: seven merged and two closed without merge.
+- I analyzed every PR that received a submitted review during August 2026. The corpus contains 244 PRs by 33 authors.
+- At collection time, 153 of those PRs were merged, 26 were closed without merge, and 65 remained open.
+- The corpus contains 701 August review submissions and 526 August inline comments across 164 PRs.
+- Automated reviewers wrote 333 inline comments: 225 from Copilot, 105 from Cursor, and 3 from GitHub Advanced Security.
+- After removing bot comments, PR-author replies, and reply comments, 40 initial human inline findings remained across nine PRs. I also inspected 17 non-empty human review summaries across 15 PRs.
+- I kept automated findings separate from human findings. Review volume is not the same as reviewer confidence.
+
+The median reviewed PR changed 6 files and 352 lines. The 75th percentile changed 13 files and 1,067 lines. This gives useful context for the two largest PRs in your history.
+
+GitHub PR metadata, files, commits, review bodies, issue comments, and inline threads are the primary evidence. Entire semantic search found the relevant commit history in `MuskanPaliwal/cli`, but no indexed checkpoint results for most PRs. PR #2162 has a locally available checkpoint transcript. Claims about the other PRs are therefore review-backed or code-history inference, not checkpoint-backed intent.
+
+## What your PR history says
+
+| PR | Result | Size | Main lesson |
+| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
+| [#1186](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1186) `docs: clarify human added attribution` | Merged after 62 days | 1 file, 33 lines, 10 commits | Documentation must describe the exact heuristic, including first-turn baselines, aggregate pairing, fallback behavior, and known exclusions. |
+| [#1359](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1359) `fix(paths): handle submodule gitdirs in worktree IDs` | Merged after 41 days | 2 files, 79 lines, 8 commits | The implementation covered several Git layouts well. Most elapsed time was review latency and repeated main merges, not a major correctness rewrite. |
+| [#1937](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1937) `fix: stop checkpoint metadata.json outgrowing github's blob limit` | Merged after 2 days | 2 files, 152 lines, 4 commits | Splitting the nested-checkout cause from write-boundary deduplication was the right move. Review also caught backend coverage and the `null` versus `[]` wire contract. |
+| [#1969](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1969) `fix: dedupe files_touched at the checkpoint write boundary` | Merged the same day | 3 files, 164 lines, 4 commits | This is a strong boundary fix: normalize where data becomes permanent, preserve serialization shape, cover both stores, and log when the boundary rejects bad input. |
+| [#1996](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1996) `fix(opencode): report transcript export failures during attach` | Folded into #1877 | 8 files, 504 lines, 2 commits | Closing was coordination, not rejection. The follow-up review still exposed a broader safety issue: export must stage to a temporary file before replacing the only cached transcript. |
+| [#2038](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2038) `fix(strategy): prevent duplicate session-end checkpoints` | Merged after 2 days | 28 files, 2,154 lines, 18 commits | The durable ID idea was correct. Review found an extra blocking lock, duplicated eligibility ladders, a lost invariant comment, and the wrong documented recovery owner. |
+| [#2052](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2052) `fix(codex): use repository hook root in linked worktrees` | Merged after 7 days | 33 files, 3,931 lines, 42 commits | This PR started with an unresolved ownership contract and grew across discovery, cross-checkout writes, migration, trust, locking, diagnostics, setup, and CI. It needed a major scope reduction before the final design became safe. |
+| [#2132](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2132) `fix(cli): show all agents in picker` | Merged the same day | 4 files, 87 lines, 1 commit | This is another strong shape: narrow behavior change, shared UI helper, focused tests, and no speculative expansion. |
+| [#2162](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2162) `fix(redact): preserve Grok encrypted reasoning payloads` | Closed after 2 days | 3 files, 39 lines, 4 commits | The implementation process was strong. The checkpoint shows real-seam TDD, a narrow allowlist, a non-exempt control, Codex collision checks, and full blast-radius verification. The PR closed because the product removed the Grok field. |
+
+Two trends matter.
+
+First, the later small PRs are materially better than the early ones. PRs #1937, #1969, #2132, and #2162 show tighter scope, better evidence, and faster review.
+
+Second, size alone is not the problem. The repository regularly merges large changes. The problem is large scope before the contract is stable. PR #2052 changed 42 times because it tried to answer discovery, ownership, mutation, migration, trust, and UX together. Once review established that Entire should inspect the root checkout but mutate only the current checkout, the design became much easier to reason about.
+
+## Mistakes to avoid
+
+### Do not patch a transition before mapping the state machine
+
+PR #2038 began with the right idea: reserve a checkpoint ID before an interruptible write so recovery reuses the same identity. The missed details were in adjacent transitions:
+
+- reservation and condensation independently decided whether a session had content;
+- the added state mutation introduced another blocking lock inside Codex's three-second SessionEnd budget;
+- a task-only session could have `StepCount == 0` and no shadow branch but still contain durable work;
+- the comment named `PostCommit` as the retry path when `doctor` owned that recovery case.
+
+Before changing lifecycle code, write the transition table. Include phase, files, transcript content, task records, durable writes, checkpoint identity, retry owner, and cancellation timing. If two functions answer the same eligibility question, make them call one predicate.
+
+### Do not decide write ownership from path proximity
+
+PR #2052 is the clearest example. Codex reads hooks from the root checkout while Entire may be invoked from a linked worktree. The first design treated the discovered path as a natural mutation target. Review showed why that was unsafe:
+
+- a derived root could become `$HOME`, `CODEX_HOME`, a bare repository's parent, or a directory outside the checkout;
+- `.codex` and `hooks.json` symlinks could redirect a write;
+- a scratch worktree could modify or remove a tracked file in another checkout;
+- an unreadable file could be reported as successfully removed;
+- repository-wide hooks could remain active while the picker classified Codex as absent;
+- a valid root-checkout configuration was reported with the same warning as a broken one.
+
+Separate these questions explicitly:
+
+1. Which file does the external tool read?
+2. Which file may this command inspect?
+3. Which file may this command mutate?
+4. Who owns migration between those files?
+5. What does the user see when the answers differ?
+
+Discovery does not grant mutation authority.
+
+### Do not collapse unknown states into absence
+
+This pattern appears across the wider August corpus and in #2052.
+
+Examples include treating every `stat` error as “file absent,” treating invalid JSON as outdated configuration that `--force` can repair, treating any ref-read error as a missing ref, and swallowing a configuration error so a feature silently disables itself.
+
+Use positive classifications:
+
+- absent means the operating system returned not-exist;
+- unreadable means the path exists or may exist, but the read failed;
+- invalid means bytes were read but could not satisfy the schema;
+- outdated means valid Entire-owned state uses an older contract;
+- unresolved means the program cannot prove which resource applies;
+- unsupported means the layout is understood but deliberately not handled.
+
+Each state needs its own output and remedy. Unknown is not absent, and skipped is not success.
+
+### Do not duplicate a decision ladder
+
+Reviewers repeatedly called out duplicated logic that could drift:
+
+- PR #2038 had two eager-condensation eligibility ladders;
+- PR #2052 introduced another Git worktree traversal beside existing `gitrepo`, `paths`, and `session` implementations;
+- repo-wide bot findings caught repeated settings loads, duplicated remote rules, and tests that copied production assumptions.
+
+Duplication is most dangerous when the code is short but represents policy. Two six-line predicates can be worse than two fifty-line formatters because a one-condition drift silently changes ownership or recovery.
+
+Before implementing Go code, run the repository's related-code discovery workflow. Search by responsibility and invariant, not only by the symbol name you plan to add.
+
+### Do not write a nearby test instead of the failure
+
+The strongest review norm in this repository is that a test must pin the production assumption.
+
+Examples from the corpus include:
+
+- asserting a helper's model instead of the remote's `HEAD`, which is the source of truth;

## The central finding

Your main risk is not Go syntax. It is changing one part of a system before you have mapped the ownership, state transitions, failure modes, and recovery path around it.

The strongest review comments repeatedly found one of these problems:

- two code paths made the same decision with slightly different predicates;
- a local fix changed behavior at a wider persistence or mutation boundary;
- an error such as unreadable, invalid, or canceled was collapsed into absent or successful;
- a test exercised a nearby abstraction but not the production failure;
- a comment, status message, or PR description claimed more than the code guaranteed;
- a new path resolver, state classifier, or helper duplicated an existing one;
- a large PR combined discovery, mutation, migration, diagnostics, and integration work before the contract was settled.

This is good news. The reviews do not show a recurring inability to write Go. They show that your next level is systems reasoning: seeing the whole state machine before editing one transition.

## Mistakes to avoid

### Do not patch a transition before mapping the state machine

PR #2038 began with the right idea: reserve a checkpoint ID before an interruptible write so recovery reuses the same identity. The missed details were in adjacent transitions:

- reservation and condensation independently decided whether a session had content;
- the added state mutation introduced another blocking lock inside Codex's three-second SessionEnd budget;
- a task-only session could have `StepCount == 0` and no shadow branch but still contain durable work;
- the comment named `PostCommit` as the retry path when `doctor` owned that recovery case.

Before changing lifecycle code, write the transition table. Include phase, files, transcript content, task records, durable writes, checkpoint identity, retry owner, and cancellation timing. If two functions answer the same eligibility question, make them call one predicate.

### Do not decide write ownership from path proximity

PR #2052 is the clearest example. Codex reads hooks from the root checkout while Entire may be invoked from a linked worktree. The first design treated the discovered path as a natural mutation target. Review showed why that was unsafe:

- a derived root could become `$HOME`, `CODEX_HOME`, a bare repository's parent, or a directory outside the checkout;
- `.codex` and `hooks.json` symlinks could redirect a write;
- a scratch worktree could modify or remove a tracked file in another checkout;
- an unreadable file could be reported as successfully removed;
- repository-wide hooks could remain active while the picker classified Codex as absent;
- a valid root-checkout configuration was reported with the same warning as a broken one.

Separate these questions explicitly:

1. Which file does the external tool read?
2. Which file may this command inspect?
3. Which file may this command mutate?
4. Who owns migration between those files?
5. What does the user see when the answers differ?

Discovery does not grant mutation authority.

### Do not collapse unknown states into absence

This pattern appears across the wider August corpus and in #2052.

Examples include treating every `stat` error as “file absent,” treating invalid JSON as outdated configuration that `--force` can repair, treating any ref-read error as a missing ref, and swallowing a configuration error so a feature silently disables itself.

Use positive classifications:

- absent means the operating system returned not-exist;
- unreadable means the path exists or may exist, but the read failed;
- invalid means bytes were read but could not satisfy the schema;
- outdated means valid Entire-owned state uses an older contract;
- unresolved means the program cannot prove which resource applies;
- unsupported means the layout is understood but deliberately not handled.

Each state needs its own output and remedy. Unknown is not absent, and skipped is not success.

### Do not duplicate a decision ladder

Reviewers repeatedly called out duplicated logic that could drift:

- PR #2038 had two eager-condensation eligibility ladders;
- PR #2052 introduced another Git worktree traversal beside existing `gitrepo`, `paths`, and `session` implementations;
- repo-wide bot findings caught repeated settings loads, duplicated remote rules, and tests that copied production assumptions.

Duplication is most dangerous when the code is short but represents policy. Two six-line predicates can be worse than two fifty-line formatters because a one-condition drift silently changes ownership or recovery.

Before implementing Go code, run the repository's related-code discovery workflow. Search by responsibility and invariant, not only by the symbol name you plan to add.

### Do not write a nearby test instead of the failure

The strongest review norm in this repository is that a test must pin the production assumption.

Examples from the corpus include:

- asserting a helper's model instead of the remote's `HEAD`, which is the source of truth;
- testing only one checkpoint backend even though the bug affected the permanent write boundary;
- unmarshaling JSON when the bug is the raw `null` versus `[]` encoding;
- simulating a competing writer in-process when production competition comes from native `git update-ref` in another process;
- testing a lock helper without proving that the read-modify-write critical section holds the lock;
- stubbing cancellation as `context.Canceled` when production wraps an `*exec.ExitError` as `signal: killed`;
- claiming a logged-out import regression while both test runs used `loggedIn=true`;
- checking that a warning and a component field appeared somewhere in a log rather than on the same log line.

A regression test needs three properties:

1. It fails on the old code for the reported reason.
2. It enters through the production seam that owns the behavior.
3. It asserts the external contract or durable artifact, not an intermediate implementation detail.

### Do not let comments and output outrun the code

Human and automated reviews repeatedly corrected comments, status text, hints, and PR claims.

Examples include a docs pipeline that claimed image externalization on a path that never ran it, a comment that named the wrong retry owner, a status that described configured behavior as active behavior, and a hint that recommended a flag the current command did not have.

Treat user output and invariant comments as code. Trace every claim to the branch that makes it true. If a message says “removed,” verify that a mutation happened. If a remedy says “run X,” verify that X can fix this exact state.

### Do not accept automated review claims without running the proof

Automated review was useful. Of 333 bot inline findings, 89 received thread replies, and many led to real fixes around cancellation, path traversal, races, user output, and test isolation.

It also produced clear false positives:

- Copilot said `range` over an integer did not compile, but Go has supported it since 1.22 and this module uses Go 1.26;
- Copilot claimed a `t.Parallel` loop-variable capture that no longer applies under current Go range semantics;
- Copilot assumed the `exhaustive` linter's `default` handling without testing the repository configuration.

Use bot comments as hypotheses. Reproduce the claim, inspect the configured tool version, and reply with evidence. Do not change correct code to satisfy an outdated model of Go.

## What to focus on more

### Build the system model first

For lifecycle, checkpoint, hook, auth, and Git-layout work, start with a one-page model:

- the owners of reads and writes;
- the durable state and temporary state;
- the transition that makes an operation irreversible;
- the retry owner after each interruption point;
- the time budget and every blocking call inside it;
- the user-visible state for success, partial success, and failure.

PR #2038 improved after you wrote this model in a review reply. Do that before the first patch, not after the fourth review round.

### Prefer the deepest existing boundary

PR #1969 is the model to copy. Duplicate `files_touched` entries could arrive from old versions or an unknown producer, so the fix normalized them where they became permanent. It did not pretend the writer was the producer. It preserved the wire format and logged evidence for future diagnosis.

When deciding where a fix belongs, ask which boundary can state and enforce the invariant once for all callers.

### Make failure semantics explicit

The repository values precise error behavior:

- use `errors.Is` and typed sentinel errors instead of matching strings;
- use `os.LookupEnv` when presence differs from a non-empty value;
- propagate caller cancellation separately from a child timeout;
- use context-aware lock acquisition when a context exists;
- use `SilentError` only when the command already printed the user-facing error;
- preserve the underlying error unless the public contract deliberately replaces it;
- never turn unreadable, malformed, or unresolved into absent;
- never report success after skipping the only selected agent or failing the mutation.

### Design tests around adversarial reality

The edge cases that matter in Entire are not exotic. They are ordinary Git and process states:

- normal checkout, linked worktree, bare worktree layout, separate Git directory, submodule, and linked submodule;
- symlinked checkout, symlinked final file, dangling link, unreadable file, and non-regular file;
- no remote, raw URL, multiple push URLs, fork, and elected checkpoint remote;
- no TTY, raw-mode TTY, `NO_COLOR`, Windows, and a missing shell;
- cancellation before a write, after a write but before state save, and while waiting for a lock;
- concurrent native Git writer, cleanup that invalidates later state, and process-global test state;
- empty queue, huge archive, nil slice, empty slice, unknown JSON fields, and older persisted data.

Use table-driven tests for classifications. Use integration tests when the contract belongs to Git, Codex, the operating system, or a subprocess. Keep tests isolated from the real repository, config directories, cache, and keychain.

### Keep the PR smaller than the uncertainty

PR #2052 shows the cost of implementing past an unsettled product decision. A safer sequence would have been:

1. Pin Codex's real hook discovery behavior with the app-server integration test.
2. Add read-only discovery and diagnostics.
3. Agree on mutation ownership.
4. Add current-checkout mutation only if still needed.
5. Handle migration, trust, and broader consolidation in separate PRs.

When review changes the ownership model, stop adding patches to the old shape. Re-scope or split immediately.

### Keep the strong habits you already developed

Several behaviors in your recent work are worth repeating:

- You split #1937 when the root cause and boundary hardening were different claims.
- You preserved `null` versus `[]` in #1969 and tested raw JSON because ordinary unmarshaling erased the distinction.
- You responded to #2038 review by writing down your full lifecycle model and asking for correction.
- You eventually anchored #2052 to Codex's real `hooks/list` behavior with a pinned integration test.
- You used red-green TDD, a control record, and cross-provider blast-radius checks in #2162.
- You kept #2132 narrow and reused a shared UI helper.
- You rejected review suggestions with evidence when the suggestion was wrong.

The goal is not to eliminate review findings. It is to move the expensive findings, such as ownership, recovery, and mutation authority, into design work before the diff exists.

## Go-specific guidance from the review corpus

Syntax mistakes were a small part of the review volume. These language and library choices mattered because they encoded semantics:

- Keep `ctx` bound to the caller context. Give a derived timeout a name such as `discoveryCtx`.
- Prefer `errors.Is` or typed errors to `strings.Contains(err.Error(), ...)`.
- Use `os.LookupEnv` when `VAR=` must behave differently from an unset variable.
- Distinguish `os.ErrNotExist` from permission and I/O errors.
- Keep atomic writes, containment validation, and symlink policy together. Atomic replacement alone does not define safe ownership.
- Preserve file modes and unknown JSON fields when editing user-owned configuration.
- Use channels, mutexes, or atomics to create a happens-before edge in race-tested code.
- Close resources at the right lifetime boundary. A cleanup method that deletes state may not be the same operation as terminating a process.
- Use `t.Parallel()` unless the test changes process-global state. Isolate Git config, repositories, config directories, caches, and token stores.
- Test raw serialized bytes when nil, empty, field names, or ordering are part of the contract.
- Check the module's Go version before accepting syntax advice. `for i := range n` is valid here.

## A practical standard for your next PR

The companion [PR self-review checklist](PR-SELF-REVIEW-CHECKLIST.md) turns these findings into a repeatable procedure. The highest-value change is simple: do not start implementation until you can answer who owns the write, what happens at every interruption point, and which test observes the real external contract.

The core GitHub searches and API reads used these shapes:

gh api graphql --paginate \
  -f q='repo:entireio/cli is:pr updated:2026-08-01..2026-08-31' \

```

item.stdout:
# Entire CLI PR review retrospective

## The central finding

Your main risk is not Go syntax. It is changing one part of a system before you have mapped the ownership, state transitions, failure modes, and recovery path around it.

The strongest review comments repeatedly found one of these problems:

- two code paths made the same decision with slightly different predicates;
- a local fix changed behavior at a wider persistence or mutation boundary;
- an error such as unreadable, invalid, or canceled was collapsed into absent or successful;
- a test exercised a nearby abstraction but not the production failure;
- a comment, status message, or PR description claimed more than the code guaranteed;
- a new path resolver, state classifier, or helper duplicated an existing one;
- a large PR combined discovery, mutation, migration, diagnostics, and integration work before the contract was settled.

This is good news. The reviews do not show a recurring inability to write Go. They show that your next level is systems reasoning: seeing the whole state machine before editing one transition.

## Research scope

This report uses GitHub data collected on 2026-08-31. August figures are month-to-date at the collection time.

- I inspected all nine closed PRs authored by `MuskanPaliwal` in `entireio/cli`: seven merged and two closed without merge.
- I analyzed every PR that received a submitted review during August 2026. The corpus contains 244 PRs by 33 authors.
- At collection time, 153 of those PRs were merged, 26 were closed without merge, and 65 remained open.
- The corpus contains 701 August review submissions and 526 August inline comments across 164 PRs.
- Automated reviewers wrote 333 inline comments: 225 from Copilot, 105 from Cursor, and 3 from GitHub Advanced Security.
- After removing bot comments, PR-author replies, and reply comments, 40 initial human inline findings remained across nine PRs. I also inspected 17 non-empty human review summaries across 15 PRs.
- I kept automated findings separate from human findings. Review volume is not the same as reviewer confidence.

The median reviewed PR changed 6 files and 352 lines. The 75th percentile changed 13 files and 1,067 lines. This gives useful context for the two largest PRs in your history.

GitHub PR metadata, files, commits, review bodies, issue comments, and inline threads are the primary evidence. Entire semantic search found the relevant commit history in `MuskanPaliwal/cli`, but no indexed checkpoint results for most PRs. PR #2162 has a locally available checkpoint transcript. Claims about the other PRs are therefore review-backed or code-history inference, not checkpoint-backed intent.

## What your PR history says

| PR | Result | Size | Main lesson |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| [#1186](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1186) `docs: clarify human added attribution` | Merged after 62 days | 1 file, 33 lines, 10 commits | Documentation must describe the exact heuristic, including first-turn baselines, aggregate pairing, fallback behavior, and known exclusions. |
| [#1359](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1359) `fix(paths): handle submodule gitdirs in worktree IDs` | Merged after 41 days | 2 files, 79 lines, 8 commits | The implementation covered several Git layouts well. Most elapsed time was review latency and repeated main merges, not a major correctness rewrite. |
| [#1937](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1937) `fix: stop checkpoint metadata.json outgrowing github's blob limit` | Merged after 2 days | 2 files, 152 lines, 4 commits | Splitting the nested-checkout cause from write-boundary deduplication was the right move. Review also caught backend coverage and the `null` versus `[]` wire contract. |
| [#1969](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1969) `fix: dedupe files_touched at the checkpoint write boundary` | Merged the same day | 3 files, 164 lines, 4 commits | This is a strong boundary fix: normalize where data becomes permanent, preserve serialization shape, cover both stores, and log when the boundary rejects bad input. |
| [#1996](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1996) `fix(opencode): report transcript export failures during attach` | Folded into #1877 | 8 files, 504 lines, 2 commits | Closing was coordination, not rejection. The follow-up review still exposed a broader safety issue: export must stage to a temporary file before replacing the only cached transcript. |
| [#2038](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2038) `fix(strategy): prevent duplicate session-end checkpoints` | Merged after 2 days | 28 files, 2,154 lines, 18 commits | The durable ID idea was correct. Review found an extra blocking lock, duplicated eligibility ladders, a lost invariant comment, and the wrong documented recovery owner. |
| [#2052](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2052) `fix(codex): use repository hook root in linked worktrees` | Merged after 7 days | 33 files, 3,931 lines, 42 commits | This PR started with an unresolved ownership contract and grew across discovery, cross-checkout writes, migration, trust, locking, diagnostics, setup, and CI. It needed a major scope reduction before the final design became safe. |
| [#2132](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2132) `fix(cli): show all agents in picker` | Merged the same day | 4 files, 87 lines, 1 commit | This is another strong shape: narrow behavior change, shared UI helper, focused tests, and no speculative expansion. |
| [#2162](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2162) `fix(redact): preserve Grok encrypted reasoning payloads` | Closed after 2 days | 3 files, 39 lines, 4 commits | The implementation process was strong. The checkpoint shows real-seam TDD, a narrow allowlist, a non-exempt control, Codex collision checks, and full blast-radius verification. The PR closed because the product removed the Grok field. |

Two trends matter.

First, the later small PRs are materially better than the early ones. PRs #1937, #1969, #2132, and #2162 show tighter scope, better evidence, and faster review.

Second, size alone is not the problem. The repository regularly merges large changes. The problem is large scope before the contract is stable. PR #2052 changed 42 times because it tried to answer discovery, ownership, mutation, migration, trust, and UX together. Once review established that Entire should inspect the root checkout but mutate only the current checkout, the design became much easier to reason about.

## Mistakes to avoid

### Do not patch a transition before mapping the state machine

PR #2038 began with the right idea: reserve a checkpoint ID before an interruptible write so recovery reuses the same identity. The missed details were in adjacent transitions:

- reservation and condensation independently decided whether a session had content;
- the added state mutation introduced another blocking lock inside Codex's three-second SessionEnd budget;
- a task-only session could have `StepCount == 0` and no shadow branch but still contain durable work;
- the comment named `PostCommit` as the retry path when `doctor` owned that recovery case.

Before changing lifecycle code, write the transition table. Include phase, files, transcript content, task records, durable writes, checkpoint identity, retry owner, and cancellation timing. If two functions answer the same eligibility question, make them call one predicate.

### Do not decide write ownership from path proximity

PR #2052 is the clearest example. Codex reads hooks from the root checkout while Entire may be invoked from a linked worktree. The first design treated the discovered path as a natural mutation target. Review showed why that was unsafe:

- a derived root could become `$HOME`, `CODEX_HOME`, a bare repository's parent, or a directory outside the checkout;
- `.codex` and `hooks.json` symlinks could redirect a write;
- a scratch worktree could modify or remove a tracked file in another checkout;
- an unreadable file could be reported as successfully removed;
- repository-wide hooks could remain active while the picker classified Codex as absent;
- a valid root-checkout configuration was reported with the same warning as a broken one.

Separate these questions explicitly:

1. Which file does the external tool read?
2. Which file may this command inspect?
3. Which file may this command mutate?
4. Who owns migration between those files?
5. What does the user see when the answers differ?

Discovery does not grant mutation authority.

### Do not collapse unknown states into absence

This pattern appears across the wider August corpus and in #2052.

Examples include treating every `stat` error as "file absent," treating invalid JSON as outdated configuration that `--force` can repair, treating any ref-read error as a missing ref, and swallowing a configuration error so a feature silently disables itself.

Use positive classifications:

- absent means the operating system returned not-exist;
- unreadable means the path exists or may exist, but the read failed;
- invalid means bytes were read but could not satisfy the schema;
- outdated means valid Entire-owned state uses an older contract;
- unresolved means the program cannot prove which resource applies;
- unsupported means the layout is understood but deliberately not handled.

Each state needs its own output and remedy. Unknown is not absent, and skipped is not success.

### Do not duplicate a decision ladder

Reviewers repeatedly called out duplicated logic that could drift:

- PR #2038 had two eager-condensation eligibility ladders;
- PR #2052 introduced another Git worktree traversal beside existing `gitrepo`, `paths`, and `session` implementations;

## The central finding

Your main risk is not Go syntax. It is changing one part of a system before you have mapped the ownership, state transitions, failure modes, and recovery path around it.

The strongest review comments repeatedly found one of these problems:

- two code paths made the same decision with slightly different predicates;
- a local fix changed behavior at a wider persistence or mutation boundary;
- an error such as unreadable, invalid, or canceled was collapsed into absent or successful;
- a test exercised a nearby abstraction but not the production failure;
- a comment, status message, or PR description claimed more than the code guaranteed;
- a new path resolver, state classifier, or helper duplicated an existing one;
- a large PR combined discovery, mutation, migration, diagnostics, and integration work before the contract was settled.

This is good news. The reviews do not show a recurring inability to write Go. They show that your next level is systems reasoning: seeing the whole state machine before editing one transition.

## Research scope

This report uses GitHub data collected on 2026-08-31. August figures are month-to-date at the collection time.

- I inspected all nine closed PRs authored by `MuskanPaliwal` in `entireio/cli`: seven merged and two closed without merge.
- I analyzed every PR that received a submitted review during August 2026. The corpus contains 244 PRs by 33 authors.
- At collection time, 153 of those PRs were merged, 26 were closed without merge, and 65 remained open.
- The corpus contains 701 August review submissions and 526 August inline comments across 164 PRs.
- Automated reviewers wrote 333 inline comments: 225 from Copilot, 105 from Cursor, and 3 from GitHub Advanced Security.
- After removing bot comments, PR-author replies, and reply comments, 40 initial human inline findings remained across nine PRs. I also inspected 17 non-empty human review summaries across 15 PRs.

The median reviewed PR changed 6 files and 352 lines. The 75th percentile changed 13 files and 1,067 lines. This gives useful context for the two largest PRs in your history.

GitHub PR metadata, files, commits, review bodies, issue comments, and inline threads are the primary evidence. Entire semantic search found the relevant commit history in `MuskanPaliwal/cli`, but no indexed checkpoint results for most PRs. PR #2162 has a locally available checkpoint transcript. First, the later small PRs are materially better than the early ones. PRs #1937, #1969, #2132, and #2162 show tighter scope, better evidence, and faster review.

PR #2052 changed 42 times because it tried to answer discovery, ownership, mutation, migration, trust, and UX together. ## Mistakes to avoid

### Do not patch a transition before mapping the state machine

PR #2038 began with the right idea: reserve a checkpoint ID before an interruptible write so recovery reuses the same identity. The missed details were in adjacent transitions:

- reservation and condensation independently decided whether a session had content;
- the added state mutation introduced another blocking lock inside Codex's three-second SessionEnd budget;
- a task-only session could have `StepCount == 0` and no shadow branch but still contain durable work;
- the comment named `PostCommit` as the retry path when `doctor` owned that recovery case.

Before changing lifecycle code, write the transition table. Include phase, files, transcript content, task records, durable writes, checkpoint identity, retry owner, and cancellation timing. If two functions answer the same eligibility question, make them call one predicate.

### Do not decide write ownership from path proximity

PR #2052 is the clearest example. Codex reads hooks from the root checkout while Entire may be invoked from a linked worktree. The first design treated the discovered path as a natural mutation target. Review showed why that was unsafe:

- a derived root could become `$HOME`, `CODEX_HOME`, a bare repository's parent, or a directory outside the checkout;
- `.codex` and `hooks.json` symlinks could redirect a write;
- a scratch worktree could modify or remove a tracked file in another checkout;
- an unreadable file could be reported as successfully removed;
- repository-wide hooks could remain active while the picker classified Codex as absent;
- a valid root-checkout configuration was reported with the same warning as a broken one.

Separate these questions explicitly:

1. Which file does the external tool read?
2. Which file may this command inspect?
3. Which file may this command mutate?
4. Who owns migration between those files?
5. What does the user see when the answers differ?

Discovery does not grant mutation authority.

This pattern appears across the wider August corpus and in #2052.

Examples include treating every `stat` error as "file absent," treating invalid JSON as outdated configuration that `--force` can repair, treating any ref-read error as a missing ref, and swallowing a configuration error so a feature silently disables itself.

Use positive classifications:

- absent means the operating system returned not-exist;
- unreadable means the path exists or may exist, but the read failed;
- invalid means bytes were read but could not satisfy the schema;
- outdated means valid Entire-owned state uses an older contract;
- unresolved means the program cannot prove which resource applies;
- unsupported means the layout is understood but deliberately not handled.

Each state needs its own output and remedy. Unknown is not absent, and skipped is not success.

### Do not duplicate a decision ladder

Reviewers repeatedly called out duplicated logic that could drift:

- PR #2038 had two eager-condensation eligibility ladders;
- PR #2052 introduced another Git worktree traversal beside existing `gitrepo`, `paths`, and `session` implementations;
- repo-wide bot findings caught repeated settings loads, duplicated remote rules, and tests that copied production assumptions.

Duplication is most dangerous when the code is short but represents policy. Two six-line predicates can be worse than two fifty-line formatters because a one-condition drift silently changes ownership or recovery.

Before implementing Go code, run the repository's related-code discovery workflow. Search by responsibility and invariant, not only by the symbol name you plan to add.

### Do not write a nearby test instead of the failure

The strongest review norm in this repository is that a test must pin the production assumption.

Examples from the corpus include:

- asserting a helper's model instead of the remote's `HEAD`, which is the source of truth;
- testing only one checkpoint backend even though the bug affected the permanent write boundary;
- unmarshaling JSON when the bug is the raw `null` versus `[]` encoding;
- simulating a competing writer in-process when production competition comes from native `git update-ref` in another process;

- claiming a logged-out import regression while both test runs used `loggedIn=true`;
- checking that a warning and a component field appeared somewhere in a log rather than on the same log line.

1. It fails on the old code for the reported reason.
2. It enters through the production seam that owns the behavior.
3. It asserts the external contract or durable artifact, not an intermediate implementation detail.

Automated review was useful. Of 333 bot inline findings, 89 received thread replies, and many led to real fixes around cancellation, path traversal, races, user output, and test isolation.

- Copilot assumed the `exhaustive` linter's `default` handling without testing the repository configuration.

# Entire CLI PR review retrospective

## The central finding

Your main risk is not Go syntax. It is changing one part of a system before you have mapped the ownership, state transitions, failure modes, and recovery path around it.

The strongest review comments repeatedly found one of these problems:

- two code paths made the same decision with slightly different predicates;
- a local fix changed behavior at a wider persistence or mutation boundary;
- an error such as unreadable, invalid, or canceled was collapsed into absent or successful;
- a test exercised a nearby abstraction but not the production failure;
- a comment, status message, or PR description claimed more than the code guaranteed;
- a new path resolver, state classifier, or helper duplicated an existing one;
- a large PR combined discovery, mutation, migration, diagnostics, and integration work before the contract was settled.

This is good news. The reviews do not show a recurring inability to write Go. They show that your next level is systems reasoning: seeing the whole state machine before editing one transition.

## Research scope

This report uses GitHub data collected on 2026-08-31. August figures are month-to-date at the collection time.

- I inspected all nine closed PRs authored by `MuskanPaliwal` in `entireio/cli`: seven merged and two closed without merge.
- I analyzed every PR that received a submitted review during August 2026. The corpus contains 244 PRs by 33 authors.
- At collection time, 153 of those PRs were merged, 26 were closed without merge, and 65 remained open.
- The corpus contains 701 August review submissions and 526 August inline comments across 164 PRs.
- Automated reviewers wrote 333 inline comments: 225 from Copilot, 105 from Cursor, and 3 from GitHub Advanced Security.
- After removing bot comments, PR-author replies, and reply comments, 40 initial human inline findings remained across nine PRs. I also inspected 17 non-empty human review summaries across 15 PRs.
- I kept automated findings separate from human findings. Review volume is not the same as reviewer confidence.

The median reviewed PR changed 6 files and 352 lines. The 75th percentile changed 13 files and 1,067 lines. This gives useful context for the two largest PRs in your history.

GitHub PR metadata, files, commits, review bodies, issue comments, and inline threads are the primary evidence. Entire semantic search found the relevant commit history in `MuskanPaliwal/cli`, but no indexed checkpoint results for most PRs. PR #2162 has a locally available checkpoint transcript. Claims about the other PRs are therefore review-backed or code-history inference, not checkpoint-backed intent.

## What your PR history says

| PR | Result | Size | Main lesson |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
